title: Count the Arguments Passed
statement:
Write a function argumentsLength(...args) that can be called with any number of arguments of any type and returns how many arguments it received.

The test harness can only pass plain data, so the tested entry point is argCountForEachCall(calls): for each entry of calls (an argument list), call argumentsLength with that list spread into separate arguments, and return the results in order. An array passed as one argument counts as one argument.

examples.why: An object, a null and a string: the types do not matter, and null still counts.
The first call has no arguments. The second gets one argument that happens to be an array of three values.

constraints: Each argument list has 0 to 100 entries of any JSON type
hints: How can a JavaScript function declare that it accepts any number of arguments?
A rest parameter, (...args), collects every argument into a real array.
Return args.length. The wrapper maps each argument list to argumentsLength(...list).

explain.intuition:
A rest parameter gathers all the arguments a function received into a normal array, so the count is just its length. Older code reads the special arguments object instead; it also has a length, but it is not a real array and does not exist in arrow functions, which is why rest parameters replaced it.

The detail worth noticing is the difference between spreading and passing an array. f(...[4, 5, 6]) passes three arguments, while f([4, 5, 6]) passes one. The same distinction shows up with Math.max(...values) and with fn.apply(this, list) versus fn.call(this, list).
steps: In argCountForEachCall, map each argument list to argumentsLength(...list).
pitfalls: Passing the list without spreading it, so every call reports 1.
Counting only truthy arguments, for example with filter(Boolean). 0, false, "" and null are all real arguments.
Flattening nested arrays. An array passed as one argument is one argument.

solutions.title: Rest parameter
solutions.idea: Collect all arguments into an array with a rest parameter and return its length.
solutions.time: O(k) per call for the spread

followups: Write argumentsLength without rest parameters, as a classic function. What does arguments give you, and why can't an arrow function use it?
A function's own length property reports something different. What does ((a, b = 1, ...c) => 0).length return, and why?
